title: PostgreSQL 19 sequence replication catches up only when refreshed
excerpt: PostgreSQL 19 can copy sequence values to a logical subscriber, but the subscriber falls behind until REFRESH SEQUENCES is run.
body:
PostgreSQL 19 RC1 finally lets a logical replication subscriber see the same sequence values that the publisher has already generated. In a quick Docker experiment the author created a publication that includes ALL SEQUENCES, synced a table with an identity column, and watched the subscriber’s sequence line up with the publisher’s after the initial copy. The surprise came a few minutes later: new rows kept flowing to the subscriber, but the sequence stopped advancing. Only an explicit  

```sql
ALTER SUBSCRIPTION sub19sub REFRESH SEQUENCES;
```  

brought the subscriber’s sequence back in step. The test shows that the new feature works for the initial sync, but it still requires a manual refresh to stay correct during normal operation.

The reader will learn how PostgreSQL 19 copies sequence state on the first sync, why the sequence can fall behind while data continues to replicate, and which command restores alignment without a full resync. The example uses only the steps described in the original article [PostgreSQL 19’s sequence replication only catches up when you tell it to](https://dev.to/alexgeorgiev17/postgresql-19s-sequence-replication-only-catches-up-when-you-tell-it-to-2410).

## Initial sync copies the publisher’s sequence value

The author started two containers, both running `postgres:19rc1`, and set `wal_level = logical` on the publisher. A table called `orders` was created with an identity column and seeded with 1 000 rows:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id   BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    note TEXT
);
INSERT INTO orders (note)
SELECT 'row ' || g FROM generate_series(1,1000) g;
```

A publication that includes all tables and all sequences was then defined:

```sql
CREATE PUBLICATION pub19pub FOR ALL TABLES, ALL SEQUENCES;
```

On the subscriber the same table definition was created, followed by a subscription that points at the publisher:

```sql
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION sub19sub
    CONNECTION 'host=pub19 port=5432 user=test password=test dbname=test'
    PUBLICATION pub19pub;
```

A few seconds later the subscriber contained the same 1 000 rows, and the sequence `orders_id_seq` reported `last_value = 1000`, exactly matching the publisher. Disabling the subscription (as a failover script would) and inserting a new row returned `id = 1001`. That single insert proved the headline claim: a freshly promoted subscriber no longer collides with existing keys, a problem that plagued earlier versions of logical replication.

## Ongoing inserts do not move the subscriber’s sequence

The next step was to keep the publisher alive while the subscriber stayed in sync. The author added 500 more rows on the publisher:

```sql
INSERT INTO orders (note)
SELECT 'row2 ' || g FROM generate_series(1,500) g;
```

Querying the publisher’s sequence showed `last_value = 1500`. The subscriber’s table caught up automatically, `COUNT(*)` and `MAX(id)` both reported 1 500, but the subscriber’s sequence still reported `last_value = 1000`. In other words, the data replicated, but the stored sequence state did not.

The author repeated the same steps on a fresh PostgreSQL 19 RC1 subscriber and observed the identical lag, confirming that the behavior is not a one-off glitch. The gap means that if the subscriber were promoted at that point, the next insert would try to reuse an already-used identifier and raise a duplicate-key error.

## Refreshing sequences brings the subscriber back in step

PostgreSQL 19 adds a new command that can be run on a subscription at any time:

```sql
ALTER SUBSCRIPTION sub19sub REFRESH SEQUENCES;
```

Running the command after the subscriber had caught up updated `orders_id_seq` to `last_value = 1500` in well under a second. The author noted that the refresh does not trigger a full table resynchronization; it only pulls the current sequence values from the publisher and overwrites the subscriber’s stored state.

Because the command is cheap and fast, it can be incorporated into a failover runbook:

1. Disable the subscription (or stop replication).
2. Promote the subscriber to primary.
3. Run `ALTER SUBSCRIPTION … REFRESH SEQUENCES`.
4. Re-enable the subscription if needed.

The author also tried the same refresh on a PostgreSQL 18 subscriber, but the version does not support `ALL SEQUENCES` at all, so the command failed with a syntax error. That contrast reinforces why the new feature matters for teams that prefer logical replication for disaster recovery or major-version upgrades.

## How the new feature compares with previous approaches

* Physical replication always copies the exact on-disk state, including sequences, but it cannot filter tables. Teams that need selective replication have historically avoided it because they cannot exclude large, low-priority tables.
* Logical replication before 19 copied rows but left sequences at their default start value. After a failover the first insert would usually hit a duplicate-key error, forcing a manual sequence reset or a full resync.
* PostgreSQL 19 copies the sequence value during the initial sync, eliminating the immediate collision. The trade-off is that the sequence does not advance automatically; a manual refresh is still required for long-running catch-up periods.

The author’s measurements show that the refresh command is fast enough to be run regularly without noticeable downtime, turning the remaining gap into an operational detail rather than a hard failure mode.

## The takeaway

PostgreSQL 19 copies sequence values when a subscription that includes ALL SEQUENCES is created, so a newly promoted subscriber will not immediately duplicate keys. However, the subscriber’s sequence stops advancing as new rows replicate, and it must be refreshed with `ALTER SUBSCRIPTION … REFRESH SEQUENCES` to stay aligned. Include that refresh in any failover or catch-up procedure to keep logical replication safe for identity columns.
